atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Australian Red Cross Society has a comprehensive risk governance structure and accountability framework for managing risk, guided by a three-lines-of-engagement operating model.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: Under the Australian Red Cross Society's risk governance model, the Board oversees management of risk, sets the tone from the top, and determines risk appetites and strategic risk tolerance thresholds.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: Under the Australian Red Cross Society's risk governance model, the Audit & Risk Committee focuses on risk, audit assurance, and the effectiveness of controls across key risk categories.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Australian Red Cross Society's risk governance model uses first-line engagement for risk control ownership, second-line engagement for design, review and challenge, and third-line engagement for independent assurance.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Australian Red Cross Society's Executive Team is responsible for ensuring effective operationalisation of the risk management framework.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Australian Red Cross Society's risk management principles include accountability for managing risks, open and timely communication and escalation of risks, consideration of impacts on quality, client and community outcomes, stakeholder confidence and trust, and organisational sustainability, and learning from mistakes and successes.

atoms.proposition: The Society does not recognise pledged donations as revenue until cash is received because it does not have an enforceable right to require donors to meet their pledges.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society recognises bequests at the fair value of the benefit received when receipt is virtually certain by grant of probate.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society recognises sponsorship revenue at a point in time under AASB 15 when the performance obligation has been met.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society does not recognise volunteer services in its financial statements because their fair value is not reliably measurable in financial terms.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society is exempt from income tax under subsection 50-5 of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1997.
qualifications: The financial statements describe the Society as a public benevolent institution.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society is registered as a deductible gift recipient for tax purposes.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society recognises loss allowances for expected credit losses on specified financial assets, including investments in debt instruments measured at amortised cost or FVOCI, lease receivables, trade receivables and contract assets.
qualifications: The allowance is updated at each reporting date to reflect changes in credit risk since initial recognition.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society always recognises lifetime expected credit losses for trade receivables, contract assets and lease receivables.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society recognises lifetime expected credit losses for other financial instruments when credit risk has increased significantly since initial recognition; otherwise, it measures the loss allowance at 12-month expected credit losses.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society normally settles trade and other receivables within 30 days.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society subsequently measures trade and other receivables at amortised cost.
qualifications: This is consistent with the Society’s business model for managing financial assets and the contractual cash-flow characteristics of the assets.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society generally settles trade and other payables within 30 days of recognition.
qualifications: The payables are unsecured.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society estimates the useful life of intangible assets at four years, with amortisation recognised on a straight-line basis.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society recognises provisions when it has a legal or constructive obligation resulting from past events, an outflow of economic benefits is probable, and the outflow can be reliably measured.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society recognises a lease asset and lease liability at the commencement date of leases other than leases of 12 months or less and leases of low-value assets.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society recognises payments for leases of 12 months or less and leases of low-value assets as an expense on a straight-line basis over the lease term when no lease asset and lease liability are recognised.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society accounts for subleases classified as operating leases by recognising rental income on a straight-line basis over the lease term.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society contributes to staff retirement funds comprising both defined benefit and accumulation schemes.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The defined benefit funds operated by the Society are ActiveSuper in New South Wales and the Australian Red Cross Queensland Staff Retirement Fund.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society recognises contributions to defined contribution retirement benefit plans as an expense when employees have rendered service entitling them to the contributions.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society determines the cost of providing defined benefit retirement plans using the projected unit credit method, with actuarial valuations at the end of each annual reporting period.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Society discounts its defined benefit obligations and other long-term employee benefits using the high-quality corporate bond rate published by the Group of 100.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Australian Red Cross Society comprises two operating divisions: Australian Red Cross Humanitarian Services and Australian Red Cross Lifeblood.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: For the year ended 30 June 2024, the Australian Red Cross Society reported total revenue of $1,090.174 million, total expenditure of $1,141.520 million, and a net deficit of $51.346 million.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: For the year ended 30 June 2024, the Australian Red Cross Society reported total comprehensive deficit of $47.324 million.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: For the year ended 30 June 2024, the Australian Red Cross Society reported total government funding of $914.531 million, comprising $785.521 million in Commonwealth operating funding, $70.691 million in State operating funding, and $58.319 million in Commonwealth and State capital funding.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: For the year ended 30 June 2024, the Australian Red Cross Society reported donations, bequests and sponsorships of $79.161 million, rendering of services of $7.802 million, sale of goods of $39.005 million, non-government grants of $13.829 million, investment revenue of $16.247 million, and other income of $19.599 million.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Australian Red Cross Society identified employees eligible for portable long-service benefits in Queensland, Victoria and the Australian Capital Territory and pays levies to the respective authorities of 1.35%, 1.65% and 1.6% of eligible employees’ wages, respectively.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society
atoms.proposition: The Australian Red Cross Society applied all new and revised Australian Accounting Standards applicable for the first time at 30 June 2024, including AASB 2021-2 and AASB 2021-6.

atoms.subject: Australian Red Cross Society

Opinion
We have audited the financial report of Australian Red Cross Society (the “Society”) which comprises the
statement of financial position as at 30 June 2024 the statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive
income, statement of changes in equity and the statement of cash flows for the year then ended, and notes to
the financial statements, including material accounting policy information and other explanatory information, the
Australian Council for International Development (“ACFID”) statements and the declaration by The Board
Members as set out on page 57 to 116.
In our opinion
a) the accompanying financial report of the Australian Red Cross Society (the “Society”) is in accordance with
Division 60 of the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission Act 2012 (the “ACNC Act”), including:
(i) giving a true and fair view of the Australian Red Cross Society (the “Society”) financial position as at 30
June 2024 and of its financial performance for the year then ended; and
(ii) complying with Australian Accounting Standards and Division 60 of the Australian Charities and Not-for-
profits Commission Regulations 2022.
b) the Society complied in all material respects with the financial reporting requirements of the ACFID code of
conduct.
Basis for Opinion
We conducted our audit in accordance with Australian Auditing Standards. Our responsibilities under those
standards are further described in the Auditor’s Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Report section of our
report. We are independent of the Society in accordance with the auditor independence requirements of the
ACNC Act and the ethical requirements of the Accounting Professional & Ethical Standards Board’s APES 110 Code
of Ethics for Professional Accountants (including Independence Standards) (the “Code”) that are relevant to our
audit of the financial report in Australia. We have also fulfilled our other ethical responsibilities in accordance with
the Code.
We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our
opinion.
Other Information
The Board Members are responsible for the other information. The other information comprises all information
included in the Annual Report 2023-24 except for the Financial Statements (financial report) from pages 57 to
116 but does not include the financial report and our auditor’s report thereon.
Our opinion on the financial report does not cover the other information and we do not express any form of
assurance conclusion thereon.

In connection with our audit of the financial report, our responsibility is to read the other information and, in

Responsibilities of the Board Members for the Financial Report
The Board Members of the Society are responsible for the preparation of the financial report that gives a true and
fair view in accordance with Australian Accounting Standards and the ACNC Act and the ACFID code of conduct
and for such internal control as the Board Members determine is necessary to enable the preparation of the
financial report that gives a true and fair view and is free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or
error.
In preparing the financial report, the Board Members are responsible for assessing the ability of the Society to
continue as a going concern, disclosing, as applicable, matters related to going concern and using the going
concern basis of accounting unless the Board Members either intend to liquidate the Society or to cease
operations, or has no realistic alternative but to do so.
Auditor’s Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Report
Our objectives are to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial report as a whole is free from
material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, and to issue an auditor’s report that includes our opinion.
Reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance, but is not a guarantee that an audit conducted in accordance
with the Australian Auditing Standards will always detect a material misstatement when it exists. Misstatements
can arise from fraud or error and are considered material if, individually or in the aggregate, they could reasonably
be expected to influence the economic decisions of users taken on the basis of this financial report.
As part of an audit in accordance with the Australian Auditing Standards, we exercise professional judgement and
maintain professional scepticism throughout the audit. We also:
• Identify and assess the risks of material misstatement of the financial report, whether due to fraud or
error, design and perform audit procedures responsive to those risks, and obtain audit evidence that is
sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our opinion. The risk of not detecting a material
misstatement resulting from fraud is higher than for one resulting from error, as fraud may involve
collusion, forgery, intentional omissions, misrepresentations, or the override of internal control.
• Obtain an understanding of internal control relevant to the audit in order to design audit procedures
that are appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the
effectiveness of the Society ‘s internal control.
• Evaluate the appropriateness of accounting policies used and the reasonableness of accounting
estimates and related disclosures made by the Board Members.
• Conclude on the appropriateness of the Board Members’ use of the going concern basis of accounting
and, based on the audit evidence obtained, whether a material uncertainty exists related to events or
conditions that may cast significant doubt on the Society’s ability to continue as a going concern. If we
conclude that a material uncertainty exists, we are required to draw attention in our auditor’s report to
the related disclosures in the financial report or, if such disclosures are inadequate, to modify our
opinion. Our conclusions are based on the audit evidence obtained up to the date of our auditor’s report.
However, future events or conditions may cause the Society’s to cease to continue as a going concern.
• Evaluate the overall presentation, structure and content of the financial report, including the disclosures,
and whether the financial report represents the underlying transactions and events in a manner that
achieves fair presentation.
